questions.question: Which of the following events is the first to occur after a neural signal reaches the neuromuscular junction?

options.text: Release of calcium ions from sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options.explanation: This event occurs after the binding of acetylcholine to receptors.

options.text: Binding of acetylcholine to receptors on the motor end plate.
options.explanation: This is the first event to occur after a neural signal reaches the neuromuscular junction.

options.text: Generation of an action potential in the muscle fiber.
options.explanation: This event occurs after the binding of acetylcholine to receptors.

options.text: Formation of cross-bridges between actin and myosin.
options.explanation: This event occurs after the generation of an action potential in the muscle fiber.

questions.explanation: The sequence of events begins with the arrival of a neural signal (action potential) at the axon terminal, leading to the release of acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft. This neurotransmitter then binds to specific receptors on the motor end plate (sarcolemma), initiating depolarization.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: During muscle contraction, the length of which of the following remains unchanged?

options.explanation: The I-band shortens during muscle contraction.
The H-zone shortens during muscle contraction.
The sarcomere shortens during muscle contraction.
The A-band remains unchanged during muscle contraction.

questions.explanation: The A-band represents the length of the myosin (thick) filaments. During muscle contraction, the thick and thin filaments slide past each other, but the length of the individual filaments themselves does not change.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Calcium ions play a crucial role in muscle contraction by:

options.text: Binding to myosin heads, enabling ATP hydrolysis.
options.explanation: Calcium ions bind to troponin, not myosin heads.

options.text: Detaching myosin heads from actin filaments.
options.explanation: Calcium ions do not detach myosin heads from actin filaments.

options.text: Binding to troponin, causing a conformational change in tropomyosin.
options.explanation: This is the correct role of calcium ions in muscle contraction.

options.text: Activating the ATPase activity of actin filaments.
options.explanation: Calcium ions do not activate the ATPase activity of actin filaments.

questions.explanation: In a resting muscle, tropomyosin covers the active binding sites on actin filaments, preventing myosin from attaching. When calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, they bind to the troponin complex. This binding causes a conformational change in troponin, which in turn moves the tropomyosin away from the active sites on actin, allowing myosin heads to bind and initiate contraction.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the role of ATP during muscle contraction and relaxation?

options.text: ATP hydrolysis provides energy for myosin head detachment from actin.
options.explanation: ATP binding, not hydrolysis, provides energy for myosin head detachment from actin.

options.text: ATP binding to the myosin head causes its reorientation and cocking.
options.explanation: ATP hydrolysis, not binding, causes the myosin head to reorient and cock.

options.text: ATP is required for the active transport of Ca++ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options.explanation: This is the correct role of ATP during muscle contraction and relaxation.
Only option C is correct.

questions.explanation: Let's analyze each option: A) ATP hydrolysis (ATP -> ADP + Pi) provides the energy for the power stroke, where the myosin head pulls the actin filament. Myosin head *detachment* from actin is caused by the *binding* of a new ATP molecule, not its hydrolysis. B) ATP *hydrolysis* (to ADP + Pi) causes the myosin head to reorient and cock (energized state), ready to bind to actin. ATP *binding* causes detachment. C) After contraction, Ca++ ions must be actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum against their concentration gradient. This process requires energy, which is supplied by ATP.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: A motor unit consists of:

options.text: All the muscle fibers in a single muscle.
options.explanation: A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates.

options.text: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates.
options.explanation: This is the correct definition of a motor unit.

options.text: A single muscle fiber and all the motor neurons that innervate it.
options.explanation: A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron, not multiple motor neurons.

options.text: All the motor neurons innervating a single muscle.
options.explanation: A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron, not multiple motor neurons.

questions.explanation: A motor unit is the functional unit of muscle contraction. It comprises one motor neuron (nerve cell) and all the skeletal muscle fibers that this single motor neuron stimulates. When the motor neuron fires an action potential, all the muscle fibers in its motor unit contract simultaneously.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: If a chemical agent were to block the activity of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction, what would be the most likely consequence?

options.text: Rapid relaxation of the muscle fiber due to reduced stimulation.
options.explanation: The muscle fiber would experience continuous contraction, not rapid relaxation.

options.text: Continuous muscle contraction (spastic paralysis) due to prolonged stimulation.
options.explanation: This is the correct consequence of blocking acetylcholinesterase activity.

options.text: Flaccid paralysis due to inability of acetylcholine to bind to receptors.
options.explanation: Acetylcholine would still be able to bind to receptors, but its effects would be prolonged.

options.text: Enhanced reuptake of acetylcholine into the presynaptic terminal.
options.explanation: The blockage of acetylcholinesterase would not enhance reuptake of acetylcholine.

questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, ensuring that muscle stimulation is brief and precise. If its activity is blocked, acetylcholine would persist in the cleft, continuously binding to receptors on the motor end plate. This prolonged stimulation would lead to sustained muscle depolarization and continuous contraction, resulting in spastic paralysis.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the sliding filament theory is INCORRECT?

options.text: Thin filaments slide past thick filaments towards the M-line.
options.explanation: This statement is correct.

options.text: The H-zone disappears as thin filaments meet at the center of the sarcomere.
options.explanation: This statement is correct.

options.text: The A-band shortens during maximal muscle contraction.
options.explanation: This statement is incorrect. The A-band does not shorten during muscle contraction.

options.text: Z-lines move closer to each other, shortening the sarcomere.
options.explanation: This statement is correct.

questions.explanation: The A-band represents the length of the thick (myosin) filaments and does *not* shorten during muscle contraction. The thick and thin filaments slide past each other, causing the sarcomere, I-band, and H-zone to shorten, and the Z-lines to move closer together.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Rigor mortis, the stiffening of muscles after death, is primarily caused by:

options.text: Depletion of calcium ions, preventing cross-bridge formation.
options.explanation: The depletion of calcium ions is not the primary cause of rigor mortis.

options.text: Accumulation of lactic acid, leading to muscle fatigue.
options.explanation: The accumulation of lactic acid is not the primary cause of rigor mortis.

options.text: Lack of ATP to detach myosin heads from actin filaments.
options.explanation: This is the correct cause of rigor mortis.

options.text: Continuous neural stimulation due to nerve degeneration.
options.explanation: There is no continuous neural stimulation after death.

questions.explanation: After death, cellular respiration ceases, and ATP production stops. ATP is crucial for two main steps in muscle function: providing energy for the power stroke (via hydrolysis) and, more importantly in this context, binding to the myosin head to cause its detachment from actin after the power stroke. Without new ATP to bind, the myosin heads remain bound to the actin filaments in a contracted state, leading to the characteristic stiffness of rigor mortis.

questions.question: Consider a single sarcomere at rest. Which region contains only thin filaments?

options.explanation: The A-band contains both thick and thin filaments.
The H-zone contains only thick filaments.
This is the correct region that contains only thin filaments.
The M-line is a protein line in the center of the H-zone, where thick filaments are anchored.

questions.explanation: The I-band (isotropic band) is the region of the sarcomere that contains only thin (actin) filaments. It extends from the edge of one A-band to the edge of the next A-band, bisected by the Z-line.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct sequence of events during a muscle contraction cycle, starting after Ca++ binds to troponin?

options.explanation: This sequence is incorrect.
This sequence is incorrect.
This sequence is incorrect.
This is the correct sequence of events during a muscle contraction cycle.

questions.explanation: Let's trace the cycle: V) ATP is hydrolyzed, re-cocking the myosin head. II) Myosin head binds to an active site on actin. III) Power stroke occurs, pulling actin filament. IV) ATP binds to the myosin head, causing detachment from actin. I) Myosin head detaches from actin.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of events during a muscle contraction cycle, starting after Ca++ binds?

options.text: (V) Myosin head is already cocked from previous ATP hydrolysis -> (II) Myosin head binds to actin -> (III) Power stroke -> (IV) ATP binds and detaches myosin -> (V) ATP is hydrolyzed, re-cocking the myosin head
options.explanation: This sequence correctly follows the steps after Ca++ binds, starting with the myosin head already cocked, then binding to actin, performing the power stroke, detaching with ATP binding, and finally re-cocking for the next cycle.

options.text: (II) Myosin head binds to actin -> (III) Power stroke -> (IV) ATP binds and detaches myosin -> (I) Myosin head detaches from actin -> (V) ATP is hydrolyzed, re-cocking the myosin head
options.explanation: This sequence is incorrect because it omits the initial state of the myosin head being cocked and incorrectly places the detachment of the myosin head after ATP binding.

options.text: (I) Myosin head detaches from actin -> (V) ATP is hydrolyzed, re-cocking the myosin head -> (II) Myosin head binds to actin -> (III) Power stroke -> (IV) ATP binds and detaches myosin
options.explanation: This sequence is incorrect because it starts with the myosin head detaching, which is not the first step after Ca++ binds, and misorders the subsequent steps.

options.text: (III) Power stroke -> (IV) ATP binds and detaches myosin -> (V) ATP is hydrolyzed, re-cocking the myosin head -> (II) Myosin head binds to actin -> (I) Myosin head detaches from actin
options.explanation: This sequence is incorrect because it starts with the power stroke without the myosin head being cocked and bound to actin, and misorders the steps of ATP binding, detachment, and re-cocking.

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is based on the state of the myosin head before binding and the steps that follow after Ca++ binds and active sites on actin are exposed.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of the myosin head during a muscle contraction cycle?

options.explanation: This sequence has the incorrect order of V and I.
This sequence has the incorrect order of I and IV.
This sequence has the incorrect order of V and III.

This sequence represents a complete cycle where the initial cocking (V) sets up the binding (II), power stroke (III), detachment (IV), and then the final re-cocking (I is detachment, then re-cocking would be the next V).

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is the one that starts with the myosin head in its high-energy, cocked state, followed by binding to actin, power stroke, detachment, and then re-cocking.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: What is the first action of the myosin head after Ca++ binds and active sites are exposed?

options.explanation: ATP hydrolysis is the step that precedes the binding of the myosin head.
Power stroke occurs after the myosin head binds to actin.
Detachment occurs after the power stroke.
The myosin head binds to actin after Ca++ binds and active sites are exposed.

questions.explanation: The first action of the myosin head is to bind to actin, assuming it's already cocked.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: What is the consequence of ATP binding to the myosin head?

options.explanation: Power stroke occurs after the myosin head binds to actin and releases ADP+Pi.
Binding to actin occurs before ATP binding.
Cocking occurs after ATP hydrolysis.
ATP binding to the myosin head causes detachment from actin.

questions.explanation: The consequence of ATP binding to the myosin head is detachment from actin.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following ions is essential for the binding of troponin to actin filaments, thereby initiating muscle contraction?

options.explanation: Sodium ions are not directly involved in the binding of troponin to actin filaments.
Potassium ions are not directly involved in the binding of troponin to actin filaments.
Magnesium ions are not directly involved in the binding of troponin to actin filaments.
Calcium ions bind to the troponin C subunit, causing a conformational change in the troponin-tropomyosin complex.

questions.explanation: Calcium ions (Ca2+) bind to the troponin C subunit, causing a conformational change in the troponin-tropomyosin complex, which uncovers the myosin-binding sites on the actin filament, allowing myosin to bind to actin.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: During muscle contraction, the energy for the detachment of the myosin head from the actin filament is primarily provided by:

options.text: Hydrolysis of ATP by ATPase on the actin filament.
options.explanation: Hydrolysis of ATP occurs after detachment and re-energizes the myosin head for the next cycle.

options.text: Binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head.
options.explanation: The binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head causes its detachment from the actin filament.

options.text: Release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) from the myosin head.
options.explanation: Release of inorganic phosphate occurs during the power stroke, not during detachment.

options.text: Conformational change in troponin due to Ca2+ binding.
options.explanation: Conformational change in troponin due to Ca2+ binding initiates muscle contraction, but does not provide energy for detachment.

questions.explanation: A new ATP molecule must bind to the myosin head to cause its detachment from the actin filament.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the changes in a sarcomere during muscle contraction?

options.text: The A band remains constant in length.
options.explanation: This statement is correct, as the A band represents the length of myosin filaments, which remains constant during contraction.
This statement is correct, as the I band shortens during muscle contraction.

options.text: The H zone disappears or shortens.
options.explanation: This statement is correct, as the H zone shortens or disappears during muscle contraction.

options.text: The Z lines move further apart.
options.explanation: This statement is incorrect, as the Z lines move closer together during muscle contraction.

questions.explanation: During muscle contraction, the Z lines move closer together as the sarcomere shortens due to the sliding of actin filaments over myosin filaments.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Tropomyosin plays a crucial role in regulating muscle contraction by:

options.text: Binding to Ca2+ ions to initiate contraction.
options.explanation: Tropomyosin does not bind to Ca2+ ions to initiate contraction.

options.text: Forming the thick filament along with myosin.
options.explanation: Tropomyosin is associated with the thin filament, not the thick filament.

options.text: Covering the active binding sites on actin filaments in a relaxed state.
options.explanation: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin filaments in the relaxed state, preventing cross-bridge formation.

options.text: Acting as an ATPase to hydrolyze ATP for muscle contraction.
options.explanation: Tropomyosin does not have ATPase activity.

questions.explanation: In the relaxed state, tropomyosin molecules lie along the actin filaments and cover the myosin-binding sites, preventing the formation of cross-bridges between myosin and actin.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: The specialized region of the sarcolemma at the neuromuscular junction, containing acetylcholine receptors, is called the:

options.explanation: The synaptic cleft is the gap between the presynaptic terminal and the postsynaptic membrane.
The motor end plate is the specialized region of the sarcolemma at the neuromuscular junction, containing acetylcholine receptors.
The presynaptic terminal is the terminal end of the motor neuron, which releases acetylcholine.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in muscle cells, involved in calcium storage and release.

questions.explanation: The motor end plate is the highly folded region of the sarcolemma at the neuromuscular junction, which is rich in acetylcholine receptors.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Rigor mortis, the stiffening of muscles after death, occurs primarily because:

options.text: There is an excess of Ca2+ ions in the sarcoplasm, leading to continuous contraction.
options.explanation: While Ca2+ ions are involved in muscle contraction, an excess of Ca2+ ions is not the primary cause of rigor mortis.

options.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum actively pumps Ca2+ back, causing permanent relaxation.
options.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum's ability to pump Ca2+ back is impaired after death, leading to an inability to relax the muscle.

options.text: ATP synthesis ceases, preventing the detachment of myosin heads from actin filaments.
options.explanation: Without ATP, the cross-bridges remain formed and locked, leading to muscle stiffness (rigor mortis).

options.text: Acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction are permanently blocked.
options.explanation: The blocking of acetylcholine receptors is not the primary cause of rigor mortis.

questions.explanation: After death, cellular ATP synthesis stops, and without ATP, the cross-bridges remain formed and locked, leading to muscle stiffness.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Arrange the following events in the correct sequence of muscle contraction:

options.explanation: This is the correct sequence of events in muscle contraction.
The generation of action potential (II) occurs after acetylcholine release (I).
The release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (V) occurs after the generation of action potential (II).
The binding of Ca2+ to troponin (III) occurs after the release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (V).

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: (I) Acetylcholine release, (II) generation of action potential, (V) release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, (III) binding of Ca2+ to troponin, and (IV) formation of cross-bridges between actin and myosin.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: The globular head of the myosin filament acts as an ATPase enzyme and has binding sites for:

options.explanation: The myosin head binds to actin, but not to troponin.
The myosin head binds to ATP, but not to tropomyosin.
The myosin head has binding sites for both actin and ATP.
The myosin head does not bind to troponin or tropomyosin.

questions.explanation: The myosin head possesses an ATPase activity to hydrolyze ATP and has distinct binding sites for both ATP and the active sites on the actin filament.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following directly causes the "power stroke" during muscle contraction?

options.text: The binding of ATP to the myosin head.
options.explanation: The binding of ATP to the myosin head causes detachment, not the power stroke.

options.text: The release of ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) from the myosin head.
options.explanation: The release of ADP and Pi from the myosin head causes the power stroke.

options.text: The hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin ATPase.
options.explanation: The hydrolysis of ATP re-cocks the myosin head, but does not directly cause the power stroke.

options.text: The binding of Ca2+ to troponin.
options.explanation: The binding of Ca2+ to troponin initiates muscle contraction, but does not directly cause the power stroke.

questions.explanation: The power stroke is directly caused by the release of ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) from the myosin head after it has formed a cross-bridge with actin.

questions.question: The functional unit of contraction in a skeletal muscle fiber, extending from one Z-line to the next, is the:

options.explanation: A myofibril is a component of a muscle fiber, but it is not the functional unit of contraction.
Myofilaments are components of a myofibril, but they are not the functional unit of contraction.
The sarcomere is the functional unit of contraction in a skeletal muscle fiber.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in muscle cells, involved in calcium storage and release.

questions.explanation: The sarcomere is defined as the basic structural and functional (contractile) unit of a skeletal muscle, extending from one Z-line to the next Z-line.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following is considered the functional unit of muscle contraction?

options.explanation: Myofibril is a component of muscle fiber but not the functional unit of contraction
Myofilament is a component of the muscle fiber but not the functional unit of contraction
Sarcomere is the functional unit of muscle contraction
Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in muscle cells

questions.explanation: A sarcomere is defined as the region between two successive Z-lines and is the basic functional unit of striated muscle. It is responsible for muscle contraction.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: During muscle contraction, the binding of calcium ions (Ca2+) primarily occurs with which protein to initiate the process?

options.explanation: Myosin is the protein that forms the thick filament but does not bind Ca2+ to initiate contraction
Troponin is the protein that binds Ca2+ to initiate muscle contraction
Actin is the protein that forms the thin filament but does not bind Ca2+ to initiate contraction
Tropomyosin is a protein that regulates the interaction between actin and myosin but does not bind Ca2+ to initiate contraction

questions.explanation: When a neural signal reaches the muscle, Ca2+ ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. These Ca2+ ions bind to the troponin subunit on the actin filaments, causing a conformational change that shifts tropomyosin and unmasks the active binding sites on actin for myosin heads.

questions.question: Rigor mortis, the stiffening of muscles after death, occurs due to:

options.text: Depletion of Ca2+ ions, preventing cross-bridge formation.
options.explanation: Depletion of Ca2+ ions would prevent muscle contraction, not cause rigor mortis

options.text: Accumulation of lactic acid, inhibiting myosin ATPase activity.
options.explanation: Accumulation of lactic acid can lead to muscle fatigue but not rigor mortis

options.text: Lack of ATP, preventing the detachment of myosin heads from actin.
options.explanation: Lack of ATP prevents the detachment of myosin heads from actin, leading to rigor mortis

options.text: Breakdown of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.
options.explanation: Breakdown of acetylcholine would prevent muscle contraction, not cause rigor mortis

questions.explanation: After death, cellular respiration ceases, leading to a depletion of ATP. ATP is required for the myosin heads to detach from the actin binding sites. Without ATP, the myosin heads remain bound to actin in a contracted state, causing the characteristic stiffness of rigor mortis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately describes the changes in a sarcomere during muscle contraction?

options.text: A-band shortens, I-band remains constant, H-zone disappears.
options.explanation: A-band remains constant, not shortens

options.text: A-band remains constant, I-band lengthens, H-zone shortens.
options.explanation: I-band shortens, not lengthens

options.text: A-band remains constant, I-band shortens, H-zone shortens or disappears.
options.explanation: This is the correct description of the changes in a sarcomere during muscle contraction

options.text: A-band lengthens, I-band shortens, Z-lines move further apart.
options.explanation: A-band remains constant, not lengthens, and Z-lines move closer together, not further apart

questions.explanation: During muscle contraction, the thin filaments slide over the thick filaments. This causes the I-band (containing only thin filaments) and the H-zone (central part of A-band with only thick filaments) to shorten or disappear. The A-band, which represents the length of the thick filaments, remains constant. The Z-lines move closer to each other.

questions.question: The thick filament in a myofibril is primarily composed of which protein?

options.explanation: Myosin is the primary protein that makes up the thick filaments
Actin is the primary protein that makes up the thin filaments
Troponin is a regulatory protein that binds to Ca2+ ions
Tropomyosin is a protein that regulates the interaction between actin and myosin

questions.explanation: Myosin is the primary protein that makes up the thick filaments. Each myosin filament is a polymerised protein with a globular head (heavy meromyosin) and a tail (light meromyosin).
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Arrange the following events in the correct sequence for muscle contraction:

options.explanation: Incorrect sequence
Incorrect sequence
This is the correct sequence of events for muscle contraction
Incorrect sequence

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: IV. Neural signal causes release of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junction. I. This triggers an action potential, leading to release of Ca2+ from sarcoplasmic reticulum. III. Ca2+ binds to troponin, unmasking active sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge formation between actin and myosin. V. Myosin head pivots (power stroke), pulling the actin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere. II. ATP binds to the myosin head, causing its detachment from actin, ready for the next cycle.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the dual role of ATP in muscle contraction?

options.text: ATP provides energy for the power stroke and directly causes Ca2+ release.
options.explanation: ATP does not directly cause Ca2+ release

options.text: ATP provides energy for the power stroke and is essential for detachment of myosin from actin.
options.explanation: This is the correct description of the dual role of ATP in muscle contraction

options.text: ATP binds to troponin to expose actin binding sites and re-uptake Ca2+ into SR.
options.explanation: ATP binds to myosin, not troponin, and is not directly involved in Ca2+ re-uptake

options.text: ATP causes conformational change in tropomyosin and phosphorylates myosin head for attachment.
options.explanation: ATP does not cause conformational change in tropomyosin or phosphorylate myosin head for attachment

questions.explanation: ATP plays two crucial roles: 1. Hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin head provides the energy for the power stroke (cocking the myosin head). 2. Binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the myosin head causes it to detach from the actin filament, allowing the cycle to repeat or the muscle to relax.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Identify the incorrect statement regarding muscle proteins:

options.text: Actin is a globular protein that forms the thin filament.
options.explanation: Actin is a globular protein that forms the thin filament, this statement is correct

options.text: Tropomyosin is a filamentous protein that masks the active sites on actin in a relaxed state.
options.explanation: Tropomyosin is a filamentous protein that masks the active sites on actin in a relaxed state, this statement is correct

options.text: Myosin is a fibrous protein with a globular head, forming the thick filament.
options.explanation: Myosin is a fibrous protein with a globular head, forming the thick filament, this statement is correct

options.text: Troponin is a regulatory protein that binds to ATP, facilitating cross-bridge formation.
options.explanation: Troponin binds to Ca2+, not ATP, this statement is incorrect

questions.explanation: Troponin is a regulatory protein that binds to Ca2+ ions, not ATP. The binding of Ca2+ to troponin causes a conformational change that shifts tropomyosin, unmasking the active sites on actin for myosin binding. ATP binds to the myosin head, not troponin.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: A patient presents with a rare genetic disorder where the gene encoding for the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) pump is non-functional. Which of the following would be the most likely consequence for muscle function?

options.text: Inability to initiate muscle contraction due to lack of Ca2+ release.
options.explanation: This option is incorrect because the SERCA pump is involved in muscle relaxation, not initiation of contraction.

options.text: Weakened power stroke due to insufficient ATP hydrolysis.
options.explanation: This option is incorrect because the SERCA pump is involved in Ca2+ transport, not ATP hydrolysis.

options.text: Sustained muscle contraction (tetany) due to persistent Ca2+ presence in sarcoplasm.
options.explanation: This option is partially correct but does not specifically address the consequence for muscle function.

options.text: Impaired muscle relaxation due to inability to re-sequester Ca2+ into SR.
options.explanation: This option is correct because the SERCA pump is essential for muscle relaxation by re-sequestering Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.explanation: The SERCA pump is responsible for actively transporting Ca2+ ions from the sarcoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is essential for muscle relaxation. If this pump is non-functional, Ca2+ will remain in the sarcoplasm, continuously binding to troponin and keeping the muscle in a contracted state, thus impairing relaxation.

questions.question: A motor unit consists of:

options.text: All the muscle fibres in a single muscle.
options.explanation: This option is incorrect because a motor unit does not consist of all muscle fibres in a single muscle.

options.text: A single motor neuron and a single muscle fibre.
options.explanation: This option is incorrect because a motor unit can consist of a single motor neuron and multiple muscle fibres.

options.text: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates.
options.explanation: This option is correct because a motor unit is defined as a single motor neuron and all the muscle fibres that it innervates.

options.text: All the motor neurons innervating a single muscle fibre.
options.explanation: This option is incorrect because a motor unit consists of a single motor neuron, not multiple motor neurons.

questions.explanation: A motor unit is defined as a single motor neuron and all the muscle fibres that it innervates.
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly explains the role of calcium ions in muscle contraction?

options.text: Calcium ions bind to actin filaments to expose myosin-binding sites
options.explanation: This is the correct mechanism by which calcium ions initiate muscle contraction.

options.text: Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to initiate relaxation
options.explanation: Calcium release triggers contraction, not relaxation.

options.text: Calcium ions bind to tropomyosin to block myosin-binding sites
options.explanation: Calcium binding removes the block, not creates it.

options.text: Calcium ions directly hydrolyze ATP to ADP + Pi in the myosin head
options.explanation: ATPase activity is intrinsic to myosin, not triggered by calcium.

questions.explanation: Calcium ions bind to troponin, which causes a conformational change in tropomyosin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin filaments (Sliding Filament Theory).
questions.subject: neet-zoology

questions.question: During skeletal muscle contraction, the Z-lines of a sarcomere:

options.explanation: This is the correct movement of Z-lines during muscle contraction.
This contradicts the established model of muscle contraction.
This contradicts the established model of muscle contraction.
This contradicts the established model of muscle contraction.
